[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding Collections, Documents, and Subcollections in Firebase Firestore"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Firebase Firestore is a flexible, scalable NoSQL cloud database designed to store and sync data for client- and server-side development. Unlike traditional relational databases that use tables and rows, Firestore relies on a document-model architecture. Understanding how collections, documents, and subcollections interact is fundamental to designing an efficient and scalable database schema."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. What is a Document?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"At the core of Firestore is the document. A document is a lightweight record containing fields, which map to values. Each document is identified by a unique name or ID. Documents can hold various data types, including strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, maps (dictionaries), and even references to other documents or geographic points."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"{
  "name": "Ada Lovelace",
  "age": 36,
  "isDeveloper": true,

}"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"2. What is a Collection?"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"A collection is simply a container for documents. Collections do not hold fields or direct data values; they only hold documents. Furthermore, collections do not need to enforce a rigid schema. Documents within the same collection can have entirely different sets of fields, though it is usually best practice to maintain a consistent structure for easier querying."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Collections group similar documents together (e.g., a 'users' collection containing user documents)."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Collections are implicitly created when you add the first document to them."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Collections cannot contain other collections directly; they can only contain documents."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"3. What is a Subcollection?"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"To model hierarchical data without creating excessively deep single documents, Firestore allows you to nest collections inside documents. This nested collection is known as a subcollection. A subcollection behaves just like a root-level collection, allowing you to add documents, query them, and even nest further subcollections within those documents."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"users (collection)
  └── ada_lovelace (document)
       └── messages (subcollection)
            └── msg_001 (document)"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Best Practices for Data Modeling"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"When designing your Firestore database, keep the following architectural guidelines in mind to optimize performance and prevent bottlenecks:"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Avoid deep nesting: While subcollections allow hierarchical structures, querying across deeply nested subcollections can become complex and inefficient."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use subcollections for one-to-many relationships where the child data scales independently of the parent document."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Be mindful of document size limits: Firestore documents have a maximum size limit of 1MB. Do not store massive arrays inside a single document."}]
